opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's obviously not adequate if you compare it to what the frontier labs are spending. We're talking about companies that raise and spend tens of billions of dollars, building data centers at a scale that's hard to even picture. LawZero started with philanthropic funding on the order of tens of millions. That's a difference of several orders of magnitude, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

But I don't think that's the right comparison. We're not trying to win the race to build the most capable general-purpose agent. That's precisely the race I'm worried about. What we're trying to do is show that a different kind of system is possible. I've been calling it a "Scientist AI": a non-agentic system that tries to understand the world and give honest, calibrated probabilistic answers, rather than pursuing goals of its own. One of the main uses we have in mind is as a guardrail, a monitor that estimates whether a proposed action by some other AI could cause harm, and blocks it if so.

A lot of the early work is about the research itself: the training objectives, the theory, showing on smaller-scale systems that this approach gives you the properties we want. You don't need a hundred-billion-dollar cluster for that. Academic labs, including Mila, have produced many of the conceptual advances in this field with very modest budgets compared to industry.

That said, there's a point where scale matters. If we want these methods to be relevant at the frontier, we'll eventually have to train and test them at scales that let people trust they work on the kinds of systems that are actually being deployed. So we will need a lot more resources over time. That could come from more philanthropy, from governments that care about public-interest AI, or from partnerships. I would actually love for the leading companies to adopt these ideas themselves. The goal isn't for LawZero to be big. The goal is for the safer approach to be used.

And I think this points to a broader problem. The resources going into making AI more capable are enormous compared with what goes into making it safe and trustworthy. That imbalance is a societal choice, not a law of nature. If governments and philanthropists took the risks seriously, the funding for safety research, both inside nonprofits like ours and in academia, would be much, much larger than it is today.

r001.rationale: The response says early research can be done without a huge cluster, but does not judge LawZero’s anticipated funding sufficient to develop a proof of concept.

r002.rationale: It welcomes company adoption and mentions partnerships, but does not propose using a proof of concept to persuade companies to fund larger systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, let's be honest about the numbers. We launched LawZero with about 30 million dollars, and we've been able to raise more since then, which I'm very grateful for. But the leading AI companies are spending tens of billions of dollars a year, and some of them are talking about hundreds of billions over the next few years. So we're not even in the same universe in terms of raw resources. If the question is whether we can compete with them at building frontier systems, the answer is clearly no, and that was never the goal.

What I try to keep in mind is that our mission is different, and that changes what adequate funding means. We're not trying to win a race to deploy the most capable agent. We're trying to do the research on how to build AI that is trustworthy by design, and in particular on this idea I call Scientist AI, a system that is non-agentic, that tries to understand the world and give honest probabilistic answers rather than pursue goals of its own. A lot of that work is about ideas, about theory, about careful experiments at a scale that doesn't require a hundred thousand GPUs. For that kind of work, the main bottleneck is talent and the freedom to think about the right problems without commercial pressure, and that's exactly what the nonprofit structure buys us.

That said, I don't want to pretend money doesn't matter. There are three things it buys. First, people. The best researchers have offers from these companies at salaries we cannot match, and we rely on the fact that some of them are genuinely worried about where this is going and want to work on safety full time. Second, compute. Even to validate our ideas credibly, to show that a guardrail actually works on models of a meaningful size, we need access to real compute, and that gets expensive. Third, independence. If we can only operate with the goodwill of the very companies we might end up criticizing or whose products we'd like to monitor, that's a conflict of interest. So I've been very deliberate about taking money from philanthropic sources rather than from the labs themselves.

And I'd add that this is really a symptom of a broader problem. Society is massively underinvesting in safety relative to capabilities. If you look at the ratio of money going into making these systems more powerful versus making them safe, it's completely unbalanced, maybe a hundred to one or worse. One nonprofit can't fix that imbalance on its own. What I hope LawZero can do is demonstrate that there's a viable alternative path, produce research that others can build on, and inform governments so that eventually public money and regulation help correct the incentives. Because ultimately, I don't think the market alone is going to fund the safety work at the level that the risks demand. That's the part that worries me, more than our own budget.

r001.rationale: The response says some research can be done without massive compute, but does not judge LawZero’s anticipated funding sufficient to develop a proof of concept.

r002.rationale: It hopes to demonstrate an alternative path, but does not propose using a proof of concept to persuade AI companies to fund larger systems based on LawZero’s approach.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to distinguish two things: the resources needed to explore a different scientific direction, and the resources needed to build systems at the scale of the leading companies. We’re certainly not going to compete with those companies on spending. And funding is a real constraint on what we can do.

But the question is whether we can demonstrate an approach to AI that is safer by design. For that, having a focused team working on the right scientific questions can make a difference, even without comparable resources. We don’t have to reproduce everything those companies are doing.

Of course, if the research succeeds, testing it at larger scales will require substantially more support. So I would not say that funding is a solved problem. The ambition is to establish the scientific foundations, build convincing demonstrations, and use that evidence to make the case for the resources needed to go further.

r001.rationale: The response says a focused team may be able to build convincing demonstrations, but it does not judge LawZero’s anticipated funding sufficient to do so; it calls funding a real constraint.

r002.rationale: The response says evidence could make the case for more resources to go further, but it does not specify persuading AI companies to fund larger systems based on LawZero’s approach.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, we have much less money than the leading AI companies, so we have to be strategic. We can’t try to compete with them on everything. The bet is that there are important ideas for making AI safe that can be explored with a much smaller budget, especially if you’re focused on research rather than building a whole commercial product.

But I wouldn’t want to suggest that resources don’t matter. You can develop an idea at a small scale, and then you need to test whether it still works as you scale up. That requires compute and people. So I think of our funding as allowing us to get started and make progress, rather than as being sufficient for everything we might need to do.

r001.rationale: The candidate says LawZero’s funding allows it to get started and make progress, but does not clearly judge it sufficient to develop a proof of concept.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions testing ideas at scale, but does not propose using a proof of concept to persuade AI companies to fund larger systems.
